verses.translation_literal: To the leader, upon stringed music, of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, with the strings to carry it: a song of David.
verses.directors_commentary: This line is not part of the prayer but the instruction tacked to the front of the scroll, like a stage direction. 'Of David' (ledavid) can mean 'by', 'for' or 'belonging to the collection of' David; the preposition does not settle which. The KJV unnumbers the line and calls it 'A Psalm of David', but the Hebrew has no word for 'psalm' here, and it says 'upon Neginah' as if that were a tune name, when Radak and Meiri read it as the common word for stringed music. The 'leader' (menatzeach) is a temple official who directed the singers; the instruction tells us this was meant to be sung with a lute or lyre, not muttered. Direct your singer accordingly: the voice rides on the strings.

philological_notes.note: The participle of natzach, 'to be pre-eminent, to lead', which names the person in charge of the music, whom English versions call 'chief musician' or 'choirmaster'. The meaning is conventional; the exact office is uncertain.

Related to the verb 'to play a stringed instrument'. The ending is pointed like a construct but is read as the ordinary singular neginah, 'stringed music' (Radak, Meiri, Metzudat Zion). Ibn Ezra reads it as a real construct, 'a song of'.

verses.translation_literal: Hear, God, my cry; give heed [to] my prayer.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hear me, O God. Hear the cry I am making. Turn your ear and listen to my prayer.
verses.directors_commentary: Two commands, two pairs of words, one thought: this is Hebrew parallelism at its barest (Radak: the verse doubles its idea in different words). It is a summons, not a request in the polite English sense: the verbs are imperatives. The first noun, rinnah, is not the KJV's 'cry' in the sense of a sob but a ringing, shouted cry, one that carries (YLT: 'loud cry'). Set it against 'prayer' (tefillah), which is the quieter word; Ibn Ezra says the cry is out loud and the prayer is in the heart, as in the story of Hannah. KJV's 'attend unto' is archaic: haqshivah literally means 'make [the ear] attentive', to prick up and listen. So the actor starts loud and ends close.

philological_notes.note: From the root 'to give a ringing cry', used of joy and also of distress. Here it is a loud cry for help, set against the more inward 'prayer'.
The causative of qashav, 'to be attentive'; it means 'make your ear alert', which the KJV's 'attend' only dimly catches.

verses.translation_literal: From the end of the earth to you I call, when my heart is wrapped [in faintness]; on a rock [that] is too high for me you will lead me.
verses.translation_dramatic: From the far edge of the world I call to you, where the land runs out and the path thins to nothing. My heart is wrapped round and weak, a cloth wound too tight about a failing pulse. And still I ask it: lead me up, up onto the rock that stands higher than I can climb.
verses.directors_commentary: Play the first line from a long way off. 'The end of the earth' is the edge of the known map: for a king it can be exile or a far front (Metzudat David has David fighting Aram, Radak has the Philistine country), and for a later exiled Israelite it is any land away from the Temple. The singer is out of reach of help and cannot lift himself, so the rock has to be higher than he is, a place where only a rescuer can set him. The KJV 'overwhelmed' blurs a physical picture. עָטַף is 'to wrap, cover', and Metzudat Zion ties it to wrapping and clothing, so the heart is swaddled in faintness, as the Targum's 'when my heart is faint' has it. Radak instead hears the wrapping as the piling up of prayer in distress. The KJV also turns the closing verb into a plea, 'lead me to the rock'. The Hebrew is an imperfect, 'you will lead me', which is a plea and a confidence in one breath. The ב of בְּצוּר is 'on', so he is set upon the rock, not merely brought toward it. 'Higher than I' is the comparative min: too high for me, beyond me. Actors should not let the voice sound like a man who is sure of his footing.

philological_notes.note: From עָטַף, 'to wrap, cover', and by extension 'to grow faint' (the wrapped-up, muffled heart). The infinitive after ב gives 'when my heart is wrapped'. Here the sense is faintness; the note draws on the wrapping image itself, not on darkness.
'From the end of the earth/land'. The commentators split on whether it means exile in a foreign country, a far battlefield, or distance from the Temple.

verses.translation_literal: For you have been a refuge for me, a tower of strength from the face of [the] enemy.
verses.translation_dramatic: For you have been my shelter before. You have been a tower of strength, standing between me and the enemy.
verses.directors_commentary: 'For' (ki) gives the ground of the petition: the speaker dares ask because the past record is good. Radak: many times you have been my shelter, and so I call. The perfect 'you have been' is a memory, not a hope. 'Tower of strength' (migdal-oz) is a defensive word, a watchtower or keep of a walled town; nobody in a climate of raiding and shifting borders hears this as poetry only. The KJV's 'shelter' is fine, but 'from the enemy' hides the Hebrew 'from before the face of' (mipnei), which pictures the enemy bearing down and the tower in front of them. The 'enemy' is singular, a collective, and the playing of the single word against many enemies is part of the art.

philological_notes.note: A place to take refuge, from the verb chasah, 'to flee for shelter'. The same root returns in v.5 ('let me take refuge'), so the verse prepares the verb that follows.
A tower of strength: a fortified tower. The image is military, and it is also a name for the divine protection in Proverbs 18:10, 'the name of the LORD is a tower of strength'.

verses.translation_literal: Let me sojourn in your tent [for] ages; let me take refuge in the hiding-place of your wings. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let me stay a guest in your tent, not for a night but for ages. Let me hide in the shelter of your wings. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: Both verbs are cohortatives, 'let me' or 'may I', and they are a wish, not the KJV's flat 'I will abide', which turns a plea into a promise. The verb is gur, 'to live as a stranger or guest', and the point is a surprising one: a person with no standing asks for the right of a resident alien in God's tent, the protected guest-status that the ancient Near East gave to a stranger under a host's roof. 'For ages' is a plural: olamim, 'ages', not a single 'for ever', which the KJV flattens. The 'tent' is the sanctuary (Radak: the Temple, or for David the tent of meeting; Meiri hears paradise). 'Wings' is the image of a bird sheltering its young, and the Hebrew sether, 'hiding-place', is more secret than the KJV's 'covert'. Selah is a mark of a pause or lift in the music of uncertain meaning; let the strings take the beat.

philological_notes.note: From gur, 'to sojourn': to live as a resident alien under another's protection, not as a native. The cohortative form gives 'let me' or 'may I'. The psalmist asks for guest-right in God's house.
A plural of olam, 'ages' or 'long times' (Radak: zemanim arukim, 'long periods'). Rashi takes it as this world and the next; Meiri reads it as the world to come.
A musical or liturgical mark whose meaning is unknown; it may mark a pause, a lifting of voice or an instrumental interlude.

verses.translation_literal: For you, God, have heard my vows; you have given [the] possession of [those who] fear your name.
verses.translation_dramatic: For you, O God, you heard. You heard the promises I made in the dark, and you did not let them fall unanswered. You have given what you hold for those who stand in awe of your name: a share, a heritage, a place of their own.
verses.directors_commentary: 'Vows' were bargains made in trouble: if you bring me through, I will do this. The singer is now at the far side of one of those bargains, so the tone shifts from asking to thanking. Ancient audiences would hear a debt as well as a gift, because a vow answered had to be paid, which is why the psalm turns to what he will do for God. Note the perfect tenses: 'you have heard, you have given'. Radak takes the past tense as a promise spoken as if done; that is a reading, not a grammatical necessity. The KJV says 'thou hast given me the heritage'. The Hebrew has no 'me'; the KJV supplies it, and the possession is that of 'those who fear your name', a group that the singer joins. What that possession is the old commentators dispute: for Rashi it is cities of their inheritance recovered, for Radak and Ibn Ezra the right to dwell in the tent or the Land, for Meiri the reward they have earned, for Metzudat David the enemy's land. יְרֻשָּׁה is land that passes by right to its heir, as in Deut 2:9, where God refuses Israel any of Moab's land as a יְרֻשָּׁה. 'Fear' here is awe and loyalty, not terror.

philological_notes.note: 'Possession, inheritance'. It is land held by right and handed on, as in Deut 2:9 ('I will not give you any of his land as a possession'). Here God gives it, so it is a gift as well as a right.
'My vows': promises made to God in trouble and paid after rescue. The ל after שָׁמַע is the ordinary object-of-hearing preposition; Ibn Ezra says it is simply added, as in 'the third to Absalom'.

verses.translation_literal: Days upon [the] days of [the] king you will add; his years like generation and generation.
verses.translation_dramatic: Days upon days upon the days of the king: add them, Lord, and add them again. Let his years run on like generation after generation, a long line of mornings that does not break.
verses.directors_commentary: The voice moves from 'I' to 'the king', and the speaker may be the king speaking of himself, as Metzudat David says, or a singer praying for him. Ancient courts greeted a king with 'may he live forever', so the hope is a formula as well as a feeling. The piling of 'days upon the days' is the sound of the verse, so let the voice stack them up. The KJV 'prolong the king's life' loses that picture and the Hebrew verb: תּוֹסִיף is 'you will add', and the line is a plea in the form of a statement. 'His years as many generations' is the KJV's gloss of the Hebrew, which says only 'like generation and generation' (דֹּר וָדֹר). The commentators differ about how long that is. Rashi and Metzudat David read it as a prayer for a full seventy years rather than death in youth (Rashi) or the years of all generations, which come to seventy (Metzudat David). Radak reads two generations. Malbim alone makes the picture extravagant: each single year stretched to a generation of seventy years. The Targum identifies the king as the Messiah, with years like the generations of this world and the next. Do not play it as a flat boast; it is a request pressed against mortality.

philological_notes.note: 'Generation and generation', the usual idiom for 'through all generations'. Here the commentators read the span differently: for Rashi the seventy years are the total, the life of one generation, for Radak it is two generations, and only for Malbim does each year become a generation.
'You will add', a second-person imperfect used as a wish. Ibn Ezra compares it to 'the fear of the LORD adds days' and says only the tav addresses God.

verses.translation_literal: May he sit forever before God; steadfast love and faithfulness appoint: they will guard him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let him sit, always, in the presence of God. And you, Lord, send them out for him: your steadfast love and your faithfulness. Let them be his watch, and let them stand guard over him.
verses.directors_commentary: The wish is for a throne without end, set in God's presence, and for guards of a different kind. A king's safety was usually his bodyguard and the walls of his house; here the guards are חֶסֶד and אֱמֶת, God's covenant loyalty and his reliability, two qualities named as if they were officers sent to a post. The verb 'sit' (יֵשֵׁב) can mean 'dwell' and 'sit enthroned', so both pictures stand. KJV 'O prepare mercy and truth' has the right imperative but archaizes it; 'mercy' is too soft for חֶסֶד, which is loyalty owed inside a covenant, and 'truth' is closer to 'steadfastness, what holds'. מַן is an unusual verb, 'appoint, assign', as when God 'appointed' (וַיְמַן) a plant for Jonah in Jonah 4:6, a verse Rashi and Metzudat Zion cite. The Hebrew has no 'that' before 'they will guard him', and the KJV supplies 'which may'. Ibn Ezra explains the gap: he parses מַן as an imperative on the pattern of צַו ('Command the children of Israel'), and the missing אשר before יִנְצְרֻהוּ is like the one dropped in 'with your heart whole' (עם לבבכם שלם). Rashi, Radak and Meiri take the same imperative. Malbim alone reads 'who appointed his loyalty and faithfulness'. Metzudat David adds that the guard is meant to spare the king war.

philological_notes.note: An imperative, 'appoint, assign', in the same family as וַיְמַן in Jonah 4:6, where God 'appointed' a plant. Ibn Ezra explains the missing אשר, which he supplies before יִנְצְרֻהוּ: 'appoint ... that they guard him'. Malbim reads it differently, as 'who appointed'.
A fixed pair: covenant loyalty and reliability. Here they are personified as guards the king needs.

verses.translation_literal: So I will make music [to] your name for ever, as I pay my vows, day [by] day.
verses.translation_dramatic: And so I will sing your name for ever, and pay what I vowed, one day after the next.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm ends where it started, with a voice and a promise. 'So' (ken) turns the whole prayer into a bargain: as you act for me, so I will answer. The verb azammerah is the one for singing with an instrument, and so rounds back to the 'stringed music' of the heading; the poem closes by naming its own instruments. The KJV's 'that I may daily perform my vows' reads the lamed as purpose, and the YLT 'when I pay' reads it as time; both are possible. 'Pay' (shillem) is a word from commerce: the vow is a debt and the daily song is the payment on it. 'Day, day' repeats the noun and carries the sense of 'every day without a break', so the debt is never cleared and the singer never finishes. Meiri reads the vow as the promise to stand at God's service without interruption, and that is the vow the whole psalm has built toward.

philological_notes.note: To make music in praise, with strings: the verb behind 'psalm' (mizmor). Its use here echoes the instrument named in the heading.
An infinitive of shillem, 'to pay in full, to fulfil', used for a debt or a vow. The lamed may mean purpose ('so that I pay') or time ('as I pay').
'Day, day': the doubled noun means 'every day, day after day'.
